analysis.one_liner: Bars internet carriers from charging websites for faster delivery or favoring their own services.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on June 17, 2014 and never received a vote, dying when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Federal Communications Commission to write rules barring broadband providers from two practices: accepting payment from a content company in exchange for speeding up that company's traffic to customers (called "paid prioritization"), and slowing rivals while favoring the provider's own streaming, voice, or other services on the same network [S2][S3]. It would have kept carve-outs for emergency communications, law enforcement, public safety, and national security traffic, and enforced the rules with civil penalties under the Communications Act [S3]. The bill never left the Senate Commerce Committee and expired when the Congress ended in January 2015 [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users benefit because their broadband provider could not strike paid deals that let some big companies' content load faster while others crawl, and could not favor its own video or voice services over competitors'. Small and startup websites and app makers benefit most directly, since they are the ones who could not afford a pay-for-speed deal and would otherwise risk being outrun by better-funded rivals. Content and streaming businesses benefit by avoiding a new toll on reaching their customers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Internet users and small online businesses

how_it_helps.text: It would ban 'paid prioritization' — deals where a broadband provider speeds up one company's traffic in exchange for payment — so websites and apps could not be forced to pay extra to reach customers at full speed.
It would also bar broadband providers from speeding up their own video, voice, or other services ahead of competitors' services on the same connection.

It preserves providers' ability to handle emergency communications, law enforcement, public safety, and national-security traffic, and it gives the FCC enforcement power with civil penalties under the Communications Act.

analysis.who_pays: Broadband providers — large cable and telephone internet carriers — bear the cost: they could no longer charge content companies for priority delivery or steer customers toward their own competing services. Large edge providers also lose the option of buying an advantage over smaller rivals, though the ban costs them nothing directly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Major broadband providers (cable and phone companies)

drawbacks.text: The bill would have barred broadband providers from charging any company for faster delivery, and broadband providers argue that such fees are one way to fund network investment and to manage congestion; the bill leaves providers to manage networks on other terms.

The bill did not touch the FCC's broader open-internet proceeding, only paid prioritization and self-preferencing, so other disputes over internet rules — such as whether the FCC can regulate at all — would have remained open even if it had passed.
Enforcement under the bill would carry a three-year time limit on penalties, shorter than some enforcement regimes, which could limit the FCC's ability to reach older violations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is straightforward: internet service stays neutral, so the price of access does not become a pay-to-play fee for websites and apps, and small online businesses keep equal footing with large ones. The direct cost to ordinary people is minimal. The strongest good-faith objection is the broadband industry's claim that allowing paid fast lanes helps fund network investment and lets services like telemedicine buy guaranteed quality; the bill's drafters addressed the legitimate-priority concern with a carve-out for emergency, public safety, and national-security traffic [S3]. Weighing it, the bill's main downside to the public is hard to see, while its main benefit — keeping the internet a level field rather than a tiered one — is real.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never came out for a Senate vote, dying when the congressional session ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 17, 2014, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The Commerce Committee never reported the bill, and no further action was taken on it after a September 17, 2014 Judiciary Committee hearing on the subject.
The bill received no vote in either chamber and lapsed when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major broadband providers benefited: no law stopped them from charging websites for priority delivery or from favoring their own services, and nothing had to change for them.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

Senate Committee on the Judiciary
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the subject on September 17, 2014 (S.Hrg. 113-845).

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out for a Senate vote.

sides.party_line_note: Only five senators ever put their names on the bill (three Democrats, one independent, and sponsor Leahy), and no roll-call was ever taken, so no record shows how the broader parties lined up.

industries.industry: Broadband providers (cable and telephone internet carriers)
industries.note: The bill would bar these carriers from charging content companies for faster delivery ('paid prioritization') and from favoring their own streaming, voice, or other services over rivals' on the lines they control. For consumers, this matters because it keeps the price of reaching customers equal for every website rather than an extra toll set by the carrier.

industries.industry: Internet content, application, and service companies (edge providers), especially startups and small online businesses
industries.note: These companies would no longer face the possibility of paying a broadband carrier for a fast lane to reach users, or of being slowed while the carrier favors its own competing service. This most protects small and new entrants who cannot afford preferential deals.
